concepts.def: The variety of life in an area.
Energy passes through food chains, lost at each level.
Carbon and nitrogen recycled through ecosystems.
Groups of a species; size limited by resources.

walkthroughs.body_html:
The Living Environment — a core area of A-Level Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Living Environment brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Living Environment.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which cycle has no significant atmospheric phase?
options: Carbon
Nitrogen
Phosphorus
Sulfur

mcqs.q: Average time in a reservoir is called?
options: Flux
Residence time
Lifetime
Half-life

mcqs.q: How are most microplastics formed in the environment?
options: They are all manufactured at microscopic size deliberately.
Larger plastic items break down physically into smaller fragments over time.
Stopping all development immediately.
Bacteria produce them.

mcqs.q: How does the Brundtland Report define sustainable development?
options: Environmental protection at all costs.
Stopping all development immediately.
Meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.
Richness is for plants, evenness for animals.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between species richness and species evenness?
options: Richness is for plants, evenness for animals.
Richness counts how many species exist; evenness measures how balanced their abundances are.
They are the same measurement.
Stopping all development immediately.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Reservoir”?
options: Pathway by which a chemical element moves through biotic and abiotic compartments of Earth.
Average time an element spends in a reservoir = reservoir size / flux.
Compartment storing a quantity of an element, e.g., ocean carbon, soil nitrogen.
Includes volcanic outgassing, biological reduction (DMS) and atmospheric oxidation to sulfate aerosols.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Anthropogenic perturbation”?
options: Average time an element spends in a reservoir = reservoir size / flux.
Includes volcanic outgassing, biological reduction (DMS) and atmospheric oxidation to sulfate aerosols.
Human alteration of natural fluxes (e.g., Haber process doubled global reactive N input).
Pathway by which a chemical element moves through biotic and abiotic compartments of Earth.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Phosphorus cycle”?
options: Pathway by which a chemical element moves through biotic and abiotic compartments of Earth.
Slow, sedimentary cycle: weathering of rocks releases phosphate; runs through life and back to ocean sediments.
Human alteration of natural fluxes (e.g., Haber process doubled global reactive N input).
Includes volcanic outgassing, biological reduction (DMS) and atmospheric oxidation to sulfate aerosols.
